people.name: Vang Pao
body: In 1975, as communist forces closed in on Laos, a Hmong general who had led U.S.-backed fighters for more than a decade left his homeland for good. Vang Pao had commanded Hmong soldiers in what became known as the Secret War. When the war was lost, he became a refugee like the families who had followed him.

Vang Pao was born in December 1929 in Xieng Khouang Province, Laos, then part of French Indochina. By Radio Free Asia's account, he was the first Hmong to reach the rank of general in the Royal Lao Army. During the Vietnam War the United States enlisted him to lead an army of Hmong and other fighters against Pathet Lao and North Vietnamese forces. The U.S. government did not publicly acknowledge the war for years, and Hmong soldiers and civilians died in very large numbers.
After the communist takeover he resettled in the United States and lived mostly in California. He remained a central political leader for many Hmong Americans for decades.

His life was not without controversy. In 2007 he was arrested after a federal investigation known as Operation Tarnished Eagle and charged with plotting to overthrow the government of Laos. The charges were later dropped. Some saw him as a symbol of Hmong freedom, and others questioned his leadership and the continuing politics of the war.

He died on January 6, 2011, in Clovis, California, at 81. Thousands of mourners attended the start of his six-day funeral in Fresno. That same day, February 4, the Army announced that a review board had declined a request to bury him at Arlington National Cemetery. In 2018 a federal law opened burial in national cemeteries run by the Department of Veterans Affairs to Lao Hmong veterans, according to a release posted by Senator Lisa Murkowski's office.
keyFacts: December 1929: Born in Xieng Khouang Province, Laos.
Became the first Hmong general in the Royal Lao Army.
1960s to 1975: Led U.S.-backed forces in the Secret War in Laos.
1975: Left Laos and resettled in the United States.
2007: Arrested in connection with an alleged plot against the Lao government; charges later dropped.
January 6, 2011: Died in Clovis, California.
February 4, 2011: The Army declined a request for burial at Arlington.

people.name: Choua Lee
body: On election night in November 1991, a young Hmong woman won a city-wide seat on the St. Paul School Board. MPR's archive records Choua Lee as the first Hmong person elected to public office in the United States. MNopedia dates her election to 1992.

Earlier that year she had become the first Hmong candidate for public office in Minnesota. By the Hmong Museum's account, she was 28 when State Senator Randy Kelly and campaign veteran Pat Lindgren asked her to run, and she was about to begin work on her teaching license. The race was for two city-wide seats against three other candidates, including incumbent Greg Filice. Hmong families had been arriving in St. Paul for little more than a decade, and their children were filling the city's classrooms.

Her win gave a Hmong woman a seat at the table where decisions about those classrooms were made. In the years that followed, Hmong Minnesotans were elected to the state legislature, city councils and school boards.
keyFacts: June 1991: Became the first Hmong candidate for public office in Minnesota.
November 1991: Elected to the St. Paul School Board (MNopedia gives 1992).
She was 28 when local leaders asked her to run.

people.name: Mee Moua
body: In a special election on January 29, 2002, voters in St. Paul's District 67 sent Mee Moua to the Minnesota Senate. MNopedia records her as the first Hmong American elected to any state legislature and the first Asian woman to serve in the Minnesota Legislature.

Moua was born in Xieng Khouang, Laos, in 1969. Her family fled to a refugee camp in Thailand and, after four years there, came to the United States in 1978, when she was nine. She graduated from Appleton High School in Wisconsin, Brown University, the LBJ School of Public Affairs at the University of Texas, and the University of Minnesota Law School, and she worked as a St. Paul attorney and community organizer before running.
She represented St. Paul's East Side until January 2011 and chaired the Senate Judiciary Committee from 2007 to 2010.

After leaving the Legislature she worked at the Asian and Pacific Islander American Health Forum and then led Asian Americans Advancing Justice–AAJC in Washington, D.C., a national civil rights organization. As its president and executive director she worked on voting rights, immigration and civil rights. She announced her departure in early 2017 after five years.
keyFacts: 1969: Born in Xieng Khouang, Laos.
1978: Arrived in the United States at age nine, after four years in a Thai refugee camp.
1997: J.D., University of Minnesota Law School.
January 2002: Won a special election to the Minnesota Senate.
2007–2010: Chaired the Senate Judiciary Committee.
About 2012–2017: Led Asian Americans Advancing Justice–AAJC.

people.name: Cy Thao
body: In the 1990s, a young artist set out to paint the history of his people. The Minneapolis Institute of Art dates the series 1993 to 2001. The result was The Hmong Migration, 50 oil paintings that tell a story covering roughly 5,000 years, from southern China to the mountains of Laos, through the Vietnam War and the Thai refugee camps, and finally to resettlement in America.

Thao was born in Laos in 1972. In 1975 his family fled to Thailand, where they spent about five years in a refugee camp before arriving in St. Paul in March 1980. He later graduated from the University of Minnesota Morris with degrees in political science and studio art.

His painting style is simple and illustrative, an intentional echo of the paj ntaub story cloths that Hmong women stitched in the refugee camps. The style also makes scenes of violence symbolic rather than graphic, so viewers can take in a hard history. In 2004 the museum gave the series a solo show, reported as its first by a Hmong artist, and around 2010 it acquired the whole series.

In 2002 Thao was elected to the Minnesota House as a DFL member for District 65A in St. Paul, serving from 2003 to 2010. The Legislative Reference Library records him as the first Hmong member of the House, with Mee Moua the first in the Legislature.
keyFacts: 1972: Born in Laos.
1975–1980: Family lived in a Thai refugee camp; arrived in St. Paul in March 1980.
1993–2001: Painted The Hmong Migration, by the museum's dates.
2002: Elected to the Minnesota House, serving 2003–2010.
2004: Solo exhibition at the Minneapolis Institute of Art; the museum later acquired the series.

people.name: Kao Kalia Yang
body: Kao Kalia Yang was born in 1980 in Ban Vinai, a refugee camp in Thailand where Hmong families waited for years after fleeing Laos. The National Endowment for the Arts says her family moved to St. Paul when she was six; MPR says seven.

Her grandmother and parents carried the family's history in memory and in spoken word. As an adult, she wrote it down. The Latehomecomer: A Hmong Family Memoir, published by Coffee House Press of Minneapolis in 2008, tells of her family's escape from Laos, life in the camp and their new life in Minnesota. The National Endowment for the Arts describes it as the first memoir by a Hmong American published with national distribution.

At the 2009 Minnesota Book Awards the memoir won in its category and took the Readers' Choice Award, and it was also recognized by PEN USA. The National Endowment for the Arts later chose it for its Big Read program.

Her next memoir, The Song Poet (2016), won the 2017 Minnesota Book Award for memoir and creative nonfiction. It is about her father, a singer of kwv txhiaj, traditional Hmong song poetry. She has since written many more books, including children's picture books that put Hmong families at the center of the story.
keyFacts: 1980: Born in Ban Vinai refugee camp, Thailand.
2008: The Latehomecomer published by Coffee House Press.
2009: Two Minnesota Book Awards for The Latehomecomer.
2017: The Song Poet won the Minnesota Book Award for memoir and creative nonfiction.

people.name: Tou Ger Xiong
body: For years, schools, conferences and community centers around the country invited Tou Ger Xiong to speak, and he made audiences laugh while teaching them about Hmong history and identity.

Xiong was born in Laos in 1973. About two years later his family fled to Thailand, spent four years in a refugee camp, and then settled in St. Paul. He graduated as valedictorian of Humboldt High School and earned a political science degree from Carleton College in 1996.

He became known as a comedian, storyteller, motivational speaker, educator and activist. He used humor to talk about growing up between two cultures, about racism and about belonging, and he spoke up for justice causes in the Twin Cities. In 2015 he helped found Hmong Minnesota Day at the Minnesota State Fair.

In December 2023, while traveling in Medellín, Colombia, Xiong was kidnapped and killed. Hundreds of people attended his funeral, including the governor, and his family created an endowment fund in his name to continue his work.

December 2023: Kidnapped and killed in Medellín, Colombia.

people.name: Sunisa "Suni" Lee
body: In July 2021, at the Tokyo Olympics, a gymnast from St. Paul won the women's all-around gold medal, the sport's top individual title. Minnesota's senators entered in the Congressional Record that Suni Lee was the first Hmong American on a U.S. Olympic team.

Lee was born on March 9, 2003, in St. Paul and grew up there. Her father built her a homemade wooden balance beam in the backyard, and she trained from age six at Midwest Gymnastics Center in nearby Little Canada.

In Tokyo she won three medals: all-around gold, team silver and bronze on the uneven bars. She went on to compete at Auburn University. In 2023 a serious kidney condition forced her to step back from the sport. She returned and made the 2024 U.S. Olympic team, and in Paris she won team gold, all-around bronze and uneven bars bronze. That brought her total to six Olympic medals.
keyFacts: March 9, 2003: Born in St. Paul.
July 2021: Olympic all-around gold in Tokyo, plus team silver and uneven bars bronze.
2023: Stepped back from college gymnastics at Auburn because of a kidney condition.
August 2024: Team gold, all-around bronze and uneven bars bronze in Paris, for six career Olympic medals.

people.name: Yia Vang
body: On July 30, 2024, a restaurant opened in northeast Minneapolis named Vinai. Chef Yia Vang named it for Ban Vinai, the refugee camp in Thailand where his parents met and where he was born. He has described the restaurant as a love letter to the parents who taught him to cook.

He came to the United States as a young child and grew up in Wisconsin, attending school in rural Wood County. He studied communication studies at the University of Wisconsin–La Crosse, class of 2010. He once washed dishes in restaurants, counting the days until he could leave the work, before deciding food was a way to tell stories.

He began cooking Hmong food for the public through pop-up dinners under the name Union Hmong Kitchen. The pop-up grew into a food trailer and then a stall at Graze Food Hall in Minneapolis. Union Hmong Kitchen’s own site says its Uptown and North Loop locations are closed and that it appears at the State Fair. He has appeared on national food programs, including the 2022 premiere episode of Netflix's Iron Chef reboot, explaining the flavors of Hmong cooking and the family stories behind each dish.

University of Wisconsin–La Crosse, class of 2010.

July 30, 2024: Opened Vinai in northeast Minneapolis.

people.name: Dia Cha
body: In the refugee camps of Thailand, Hmong women stitched paj ntaub, or story cloths, embroidered with scenes of village life, war and escape across the Mekong River. Dia Cha carried that form into American classrooms. Her 1996 children's book, Dia's Story Cloth, uses a cloth stitched in 1990 in a Thai refugee camp by her aunt and uncle, Chue and Nhia Thao Cha, to tell her family's journey.

Cha was born in Laos. In 1975 she left with her family for Thailand and lived in a refugee camp until coming to the United States in 1979. She began formal classroom study in ninth grade and graduated four years later from Abraham Lincoln High School in Denver. She earned a B.A. in anthropology from Metropolitan State College in Denver in 1989, an M.A. in applied anthropology from Northern Arizona University in 1992, and a doctorate in anthropology from the University of Colorado Boulder in 2000.
An author note dated 2006, posted by Legacies of War, lists her on the anthropology and ethnic studies faculty at St. Cloud State University in Minnesota. We could not confirm her current position.

Her scholarship includes Hmong American Concepts of Health, Healing, and Conventional Medicine (Routledge, 2003), which grew out of her dissertation. She also co-wrote collections of Hmong folk stories for teachers with Norma Livo.

people.name: Kou Yang
body: Kou Yang arrived in the United States as a refugee in 1976 with only a few words of English, and his first job was washing dishes at a French restaurant in New Orleans. He finished his working life as a professor emeritus.

He was born in 1954 in a remote village in northern Laos, and he spent a year in a Thai refugee camp before resettling. He earned an associate degree from Long Beach City College (1982), then a bachelor's (1987) and a master's in social work (1991) from California State University, Fresno. In 1995 he earned an Ed.D. in educational leadership from the joint doctoral program of Fresno State and the University of California, Davis.

Before teaching he worked for years as a social worker, for Los Angeles County from 1980 to 1984 and then in Fresno and Tulare County services. He taught ethnic studies at California State University, Stanislaus, from 1998 to 2013. In 2001 he created a course there on the Hmong experience in the United States, which continues as The Hmong American Experience.
He died on February 6, 2021. Hmong American Experience, which published a detailed tribute, remembered him as a pioneer and scholar.

1976: Arrived in the U.S. as a refugee.
1991: MSW, Fresno State; 1995: Ed.D., Fresno State and UC Davis joint program.

people.name: Lee Pao Xiong
body: In the early 2000s, Concordia University in St. Paul opened a center dedicated to Hmong history, culture and research. Its founding director was Lee Pao Xiong. He was born in 1966 in Long Tieng, Laos, the base of Hmong forces during the Secret War, where his father served in the Hmong army. After Long Tieng fell in May 1975, the family spent more than a year in Thai refugee camps. They came to the United States in 1976, settled first in Indiana, and moved to the Twin Cities in 1979. He earned a B.S. from the University of Minnesota and an M.A. from Hamline University.

Before academia he led the Hmong Youth Association of Minnesota, Hmong American Partnership and the State Council on Asian-Pacific Minnesotans. He served as president and CEO of The Urban Coalition and as director of housing policy and development for the City of Minneapolis. From 1997 to 2003 he sat on the Metropolitan Council after Governor Jesse Ventura appointed him, and he co-chaired committees that coordinated planning for the Central Corridor, now the Green Line on University Avenue.

In 2000, President Bill Clinton appointed him to the President's Advisory Commission on Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders. The Minnesota Opera's biography describes this as making him the first Hmong presidential appointee in the nation.

He also co-founded the Hmong Resource Fair, the Asian Festival (now St. Paul's Dragon Boat Festival), Hmong Academy (now Hmong College Prep Academy), the Hmong Community School of Excellence and the Asian Development Corporation (now the Asian Economic Development Association).
In October 2025, Concordia marked his departure after more than two decades and said he would serve as vice president of strategy and external affairs at Keystone Community Partners.
keyFacts: 1966: Born in Long Tieng, Laos.
1976: Arrived in the U.S.; moved to the Twin Cities in 1979.
1997–2003: Metropolitan Council member.
2000: Appointed to the President's Advisory Commission on Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders.
Founding director of the Center for Hmong Studies at Concordia University, St. Paul.

people.name: Bee Vang
body: In the summer of 2008, a Minnesota teenager who had never acted flew to Detroit to begin filming opposite Clint Eastwood. Bee Vang had auditioned on a whim. More than 2,000 young people had competed for the part, and he learned he had won it only a week before shooting began.

The film was Gran Torino. Eastwood plays a retired autoworker whose Detroit neighborhood has filled with Hmong families, and Vang plays Thao, the shy teenager next door. Very few professional Hmong actors belonged to the Screen Actors Guild, so the casting director, Ellen Chenoweth, and her team reached out to Hmong communities around the country and recruited people who had never acted. The film opened in New York and Los Angeles on December 12, 2008, and nationwide in January 2009.

Vang was born in Fresno, California. His parents were born in Laos, lived in Thailand, and came to the United States around 1987. The family moved to Minnesota when he was a toddler, and he was 16 and in high school during filming.
In the years that followed he spoke publicly about how the film depicted Hmong people, and he questioned whether it deserved its reputation as groundbreaking.
keyFacts: Born in Fresno, California; family moved to Minnesota when he was a toddler.
2008: Cast as Thao in Gran Torino at 16, with no prior acting experience.

people.name: Tou SaiKo Lee
body: On stages in the Twin Cities, a young rapper and his grandmother traded verses. Tou SaiKo Lee rapped in English. His grandmother, Youa Chang, answered in Hmong with kwv txhiaj, the traditional song poetry she performed from memory. She could not read or write, and she carried a large body of poetry in her head. They performed together for about ten years, until she died in 2017.

Lee was raised in Minnesota after his parents came from Laos in 1979. Hmong was his first language, and he lost much of it once he started kindergarten in English. As a teenager he began writing hip-hop and performing spoken word around Minneapolis and St. Paul. He described it to NPR as a way to have a voice in the United States.

The idea to perform with his grandmother came after a local theater event encouraged Hmong artists to collaborate. Lee later learned that she had been wounded by landmine shrapnel in Laos after the war.

For more than 20 years he has led spoken word, storytelling and hip-hop residencies in schools and community groups across five states. He founded Street Stops and Mountain Tops, which connects Minnesota teaching artists with students in Hmong villages in Thailand. In 2016 he received a Bush Foundation Leadership Fellowship. He earned a master's in Southeast Asian Studies from the University of Wisconsin–Madison and teaches Worldview Through Hmong Language at Metropolitan State University in St. Paul. He has been writing a memoir titled My Grandma Can Freestyle.

people.name: Gia Vang
body: When St. Paul celebrated Olympic gymnast Suni Lee, the emcee of the community celebration was a familiar face on Twin Cities morning television: Gia Vang, co-host of KARE 11 Sunrise. Twin Cities Business described her as the first Hmong American television anchor in the Twin Cities.

Vang was born in Modesto, California, and raised in Sacramento. She earned a journalism degree from Sacramento State University and worked her way up through local markets: Kansas City, Phoenix and Fresno.

In 2019 she moved to KARE 11. During her years in Minnesota she covered the trials of Derek Chauvin and Kim Potter and Suni Lee's Olympic Games. KARE 11 Sunrise won a regional Emmy, and Twin Cities Business named her to its 2022 TCB 100.

In July 2022 NBC Bay Area announced that she was joining it. As of October 2026, she anchors its weekend evening news and reports from San Francisco. NBC describes her as the first Hmong American news anchor in a major media market. With journalist Michelle Li, she co-founded the Very Asian Foundation.

people.name: Mai Thor
body: Mai Thor is a Hmong refugee from Laos who contracted polio as a young child and uses a wheelchair. She describes herself as a disabled Hmong woman and a disability justice advocate, and she has worked in disability rights for more than 20 years.

She has worked at the Minnesota Department of Health, as civic engagement coordinator at the Minnesota Department of Human Rights, and as a program manager at the Minnesota Department of Transportation leading transit and street-access work. As a 2021 Bush Fellow she studied ableism, disability culture, history and law, with the goal of bringing disability justice into social and racial justice movements. She joined the board of the Metropolitan Center for Independent Living in 2024.

As of February 2026 she is chief program officer at The Arc Minnesota, and that month the Minnesota Council on Disability reported that she received the Champion of Change Award from the Governor's Council on the Martin Luther King Jr. Holiday.

In a 2024 interview she said that "disability is so taboo in the Hmong community," speaking from her own experience, and that she wants families to know that it is okay to have a disability. She also said it took her a long time to become comfortable with who she is.

people.name: Houa Moua
body: Houa Moua is a comedian, actor, educational assistant and disability-justice advocate who uses a wheelchair. She told Sahan Journal that she lived in denial about her disability for her first two decades, and that special education classes made her feel othered.
In her early 20s she learned more about her disability and built friendships with other disabled people, especially Hmong women. She co-founded United Hmong with Disabilities.

She uses humor to take on stereotypes. She performed at the Walker Art Center's Green Roof Poetry in 2022, and her comedy set Living Inspirationally ran on the first day of the group's 2026 photo exhibit at the Walker. She has spoken about everyday barriers, such as getting stuck in snow near a Frogtown restaurant and festival food stalls that could be reached only up a hill.

Comedian and actor; educational assistant.
Performed at Walker Art Center events in 2022 and 2026.

institutions.name: Center for Hmong Studies, Concordia University, St. Paul
institutions.type: University research center, library and archive
body: The Center for Hmong Studies gave Hmong history and culture an academic home in St. Paul. A February 2009 announcement said the center had been operating for almost five years, which puts its start around 2004. Lee Pao Xiong was its founding director.

By 2009 it had held two International Conferences on Hmong Studies, hosted more than ten lectures, co-produced two documentary films and started a minor in Hmong studies. Visiting scholars included Dr. Gary Yia Lee of Australia as its first scholar-in-residence and a Fulbright scholar from Guizhou University in China. It signed exchange and joint research agreements with Guizhou University and Guizhou University for Nationalities.

Concordia's library page for the center, updated in August 2026, describes a research collection of books, papers, documents, artifacts and recordings, and six international conferences so far. It says the center is in a period of transition, and it names a library director as the contact.
keyFacts: About 2004: Began operating.
Founding director: Lee Pao Xiong, who left in 2025.
Six International Conferences on Hmong Studies.
August 2026: Concordia describes the center as in a period of transition.
institutions.connectToWork: Before your team writes about a community's history, what would you ask a scholar from that community to read, and how would you pay for their time?

institutions.name: Hmong Museum
institutions.location: Hmong Village Shopping Center, 1001 Johnson Parkway, B22, St. Paul
body: The Hmong Museum says it was founded in 2015. Its founder and executive director is Mai Vang Huizel, who previously worked as a museum registrar, curator and collections manager. Its stated mission is deepening connection to and appreciation of Hmong American history and heritage through collaborative initiatives, educational programs and intergenerational healing.

In 2020 it received a $76,955 grant from Minnesota's Arts and Cultural Heritage Fund, administered by the Minnesota Humanities Center, to develop a traveling exhibit on Hmong oral culture: history narratives, skills taught by word and example, and folktales. The exhibit was designed to invite visitors to share their own stories.

The museum now runs a gallery at Hmong Village on St. Paul's East Side, open on weekends. It offers exhibits, group visits, a journal called Peb Li and online story maps, including one about Choua Lee.
keyFacts: 2015: Founded by Mai Vang Huizel, its executive director.
July 2020 to June 2022: $76,955 state grant for a traveling exhibit on oral culture.
Gallery open Saturdays and Sundays at Hmong Village.
institutions.connectToWork: If your team visited a place like this before planning outreach, what would you want to learn there, and what would you bring back to change?

institutions.name: Hmongtown Marketplace
body: At Hmongtown Marketplace, shoppers can find fresh produce and ready-to-eat dishes such as papaya salad and roasted meat, along with Hmong clothing, jewelry and everyday goods.

Entrepreneur Toua Xiong founded the market in 2004 on a six-acre former lumberyard in St. Paul's Frogtown neighborhood. Its design draws on the open-air markets of Chiang Mai, Thailand, and Vientiane, Laos. APIA Every Day calls it the first Hmong-owned and operated market in the United States.

The market has two buildings and an open-air area. Meet Minneapolis counts more than 200 vendors, while the market's own site lists over 125 stores, including 11 restaurants. With Hmong Village on the East Side, it is part of the Little Mekong Cultural District.

The market's site lists hours of 9 a.m. to 7 p.m. daily, and says temporary hours have been in effect since January 17, 2026, because of community safety concerns. As of October 7, 2026, MPR News reports that Stearns Bank is suing over about $6.6 million, a receiver hearing is set for Nov. 24, 2026, and the market could close.
keyFacts: 2004: Founded by Toua Xiong.
Six-acre former lumberyard in Frogtown.
Over 125 stores by its own count; more than 200 vendors by Meet Minneapolis's.
Part of the Little Mekong Cultural District.

institutions.name: United Hmong with Disabilities
institutions.type: Nonprofit led by Hmong disabled people
body: United Hmong with Disabilities is a St. Paul nonprofit led by Hmong disabled people. Houa Moua is a co-founder and Sue Yang is board president. IRS records show nonprofit status from January 2024.

In 2026 the group created Many Ways of Being: Hmong Disability Stories in Photos. The exhibit profiles eight Hmong people of different ages with visible and invisible disabilities. It opened at Hmong Village in St. Paul in April 2026 and was shown at the Walker Art Center in May 2026. Sue Yang told Sahan Journal that the idea was to show that people with disabilities are like ordinary people.
keyFacts: Based in St. Paul.
January 2024: IRS nonprofit status.
April and May 2026: Photo exhibit at Hmong Village and the Walker Art Center.

disability.intro: This is background for preparing questions. It does not describe any person or family. Hmong people in Minnesota differ widely in faith, generation, education and time in the U.S. The main Minnesota source here is one 2014 state report. It interviewed 15 Hmong parents of autistic children, it covers autism only, and the interviews are more than ten years old. We did not find a Minnesota study of how Hmong adults with other disabilities understand disability. The rest comes from what Hmong disabled advocates have said in public.
questions: What words does your family use to talk about what is going on? How do you explain it to relatives?
Has anyone given you a diagnosis or a label? Do you agree with it, and has it helped or got in the way?
What would you want a disability label or assessment to open up for you? Is there anything you want it to avoid?
Who else in your family helps make decisions or give care? Would you like them included?
Is your family doing anything else to help, such as ceremonies or church? How can we work around that?
Would you rather meet one-on-one, or would you like to meet other parents or disabled people too?
What gets in the way right now: work schedules, other children, transportation, cost, or waiting?
Would you like respite or care from someone who speaks Hmong?
Would you like an interpreter, and do you want information spoken, written or shown in pictures?
What would you like me to call this, and do you prefer "disabled person", "person with a disability" or other words?
Is there anything about how this started that you would like me to know?

context.heading: What the 2014 study heard about autism
body: The Minnesota Department of Health report compared immigrant groups and included 15 individual interviews with Hmong parents. They most often described autism as a medical, genetic or neurological condition. Next, in order, came unclear what autism is, a developmental condition, a spiritual concern, and a mental illness. Parents could hold more than one view at once. Vaccines did not emerge as a central concern among the Hmong parents, unlike among Somali parents.

Many Hmong parents in the study said they had never heard of autism before. One said, "we don't have a term for autism in Hmong." For some, the child's soul or spirit was part of how they saw it. One parent said the grandparents connected a grandson's delays to his name and wanted a hu plig, a soul-calling ceremony, and a name change, while the parent pursued a medical diagnosis.

A 2014 master's thesis interviewed two Hmong families, with no location stated, and found that both Western medical beliefs and Hmong beliefs and values shaped how they understood autism. Two families cannot speak for others.

sources.label: Minnesota Department of Health, A Qualitative Study of Families of Children with Autism in the Somali Community: Comparing the Experiences of Immigrant Groups (2014)
Moua, A qualitative interview study of Hmong families making sense of their children with autism (Mills College, 2014), abstract

context.heading: Family, caregiving and load
body: Parents in the study had on average more than four children, and 31 percent were single-parent households. Among those born abroad, average time in the U.S. was about 24 years, and 64 percent reported more than a high school education. These figures describe 15 parents, not Hmong families generally.

Parents named work, lack of time and caring for several children as reasons a child was identified later. One parent described depression and hospital stays linked to caregiving stress. The authors also wrote that the parents they met were not passive: they often noticed differences first and sought help.
We did not find research on how clans, shamans or gender roles shape disability decisions, so this page does not describe them. Ask.

sources.label: Minnesota Department of Health, A Qualitative Study of Families of Children with Autism in the Somali Community: Comparing the Experiences of Immigrant Groups (2014)

context.heading: Stigma and what people have said about it
body: The report says that among Hmong parents, stigma was associated with a belief that a family may be genetically flawed or cursed for having a child with a disability. One parent said the community may frown on a family and ask what the mother did wrong. Some parents described waiting to see whether a child would improve. Another said there is nothing you can do but love him.

Hmong disabled adults have spoken about this directly. Sue Yang told Sahan Journal in 2026 that her parents once said her disability came from a curse. Mai Thor said in 2024 that disability is taboo in the Hmong community and that families should know it is okay. These are individual accounts. Avoid blame-oriented language about cause.

sources.label: Minnesota Department of Health, A Qualitative Study of Families of Children with Autism in the Somali Community: Comparing the Experiences of Immigrant Groups (2014)
Sahan Journal, Hmong photo exhibit at Walker Art Center reframes disability and identity (May 7, 2026)
MPR News and Sahan Journal, Hmong disability advocate connects inclusivity and accessibility (July 10, 2024)

context.heading: System barriers and what helps
body: Wait lists were the problem Hmong parents named most, followed by insurance and cost, a complicated system, and transportation. Interpreter gaps came up too. Family support services and counseling ranked first among the services Hmong parents said they needed, and parents talked about wanting to know other parents who shared their experience. The study found parents preferred respite from people who shared their language and understood autism, or went without.
Explain wait lists, timelines and costs up front, and check in while a family waits. Check these system explanations before reading a missed appointment as cultural.

sources.label: Minnesota Department of Health, A Qualitative Study of Families of Children with Autism in the Somali Community: Comparing the Experiences of Immigrant Groups (2014)

context.heading: Words, language and how to work
body: Legal and advocacy publications in Hmong use xiam oob qhab for disability, also spelled xiam oos qhab or xiam oob khab. We could not confirm a word-by-word meaning. Houa Moua told Sahan Journal that the vocabulary around disability is all very negative and describes it mainly as a loss, and that deaf or autistic people may be called a word meaning dumb.

Follow each person's own language: Mai Thor calls herself a disabled Hmong woman, and United Hmong with Disabilities uses a different phrasing. Use a trained interpreter, not a child or relative. About half of the Hmong interviews in the study were held in Hmong. Some terms have no direct equivalent, so ask the interpreter to describe the concept and check that it was understood. Ask which format the person wants.

context.heading: Healing, faith and formal services
body: The interviews show ceremonies and medical or educational services used in the same family. Ask what the family is already doing, do not frame a ceremony as competing with services, and schedule around family or ceremonial events when asked. We did not find sources on the role of shamans or Christian churches in disability care, so this page does not describe one.

Hmong disabled leadership is visible in Minnesota. Mai Thor and Houa Moua are profiled on this page, and United Hmong with Disabilities is led by disabled Hmong people. Do not treat any one person or organization as speaking for everyone.

organizations.intro: MPR News said in March 2024, citing recent census figures, that more than 95,000 Hmong people live in Minnesota and more than half live in Ramsey County. That count does not tell you who a person is or who speaks for them. Organizations below include a clan council, social-service nonprofits, cultural and arts groups, farmer and business networks, and media in Hmong and English. The list below is not complete, and listing here says nothing about who a person trusts.

entries.name: Hmong American Partnership
entries.type: Social services, workforce and community development
entries.location: St. Paul, main office at 1075 Arcade Street
entries.purpose: Says it serves more than 25,000 immigrants and refugees in the Twin Cities. Programs include HAP Academy OIC career and technical education, adult basic education, business support, and help enrolling in health insurance and SNAP.

entries.name: Hmong 18 Council
entries.purpose: A nonprofit whose stated mission includes social justice, traditional values and practices, and developing emerging leaders. In March 2024 its president told MPR News that it was designing the state's first Hmong community hub, with $3 million from the Legislature and a $600,000 match to raise; the same report expected it to open around the end of 2025. Confirm the current status before referring anyone. Its 2022–2023 project recorded elders' accounts of clan customs.

entries.name: Hmong Cultural Center
entries.location: St. Paul, 375 University Avenue West, Suite 204
entries.purpose: Founded in 1992. Offers free ESL and citizenship classes, cultural arts education, online classes on Hmong history and culture, a speaker's bureau and the Hmong Resource Center Library. Its museum, the Hmong Cultural Center Museum, opened in 2014 and added expanded exhibits in December 2021.

entries.name: Center for Hmong Arts and Talent
entries.purpose: Says it nurtures and explores the Hmong American experience through artistic expression, with music and dance lessons, fashion design mentorship, theater and youth development. A state grant record shows a fall 2024 fashion show, and it filed with the IRS for 2023. Confirm current programs before referring anyone.

entries.name: Hmong American Farmers Association
entries.purpose: Founded in 2011 by Hmong farming families. Builds the prosperity of Hmong farmers through cooperative work and advocacy, and runs a CSA, wholesale sales, a shared farm and farm tours.

entries.name: Hnub Tshiab: Hmong Women Achieving Together
entries.purpose: Says it is the longest-standing organization nationally led by and serving Hmong women. Names a Hmong Woman of the Year, holds the Living Our Dreams Gala, and is leading a campaign for a planned Hmong Women's Center in the Twin Cities.

entries.name: Minnesota Hmong Chamber of Commerce
entries.purpose: Says it empowers Hmong-owned businesses through engagement, collaboration and advocacy. MPR News reported in 2016 that it had started nearly two decades earlier and was being revived. Confirm that it is currently active before referring anyone.

entries.name: Hmong Alliance churches
entries.location: Twin Cities and Walnut Grove congregations
entries.purpose: Christian and Missionary Alliance congregations in Maplewood, St. Paul, Brooklyn Center, Coon Rapids, Spring Lake Park and Walnut Grove, listed by the denomination's Hmong District, which is based in Thornton, Colorado, and marked its 40th year in 2018. These congregations are one faith route among several.
aliases: Christian and Missionary Alliance, Hmong District

entries.name: Lao Family Community of Minnesota
entries.location: St. Paul, 320 University Avenue West, per IRS records
entries.purpose: A St. Paul nonprofit with IRS status since 1983 and a filing for 2023, showing modest revenue. We could not confirm current programs from its website. Call before referring anyone.
entries.linkLabel: IRS filings on ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer

entries.name: Hmong College Prep Academy
entries.purpose: A K–12 charter school with Hmong language and culture classes. In 2019 it lost more than $4 million in a hedge fund investment that, KSTP reported, a state auditor's report found broke state law.

entries.name: Hmong Archives
entries.location: St. Paul, collections at East Side Freedom Library, 1105 Greenbrier Street
entries.purpose: A nonprofit collecting and sharing the history and culture of the Hmong people since February 1999: documents, books, photos, recordings, newspapers and objects. Tours by appointment.

entries.name: Hmong National Development
entries.purpose: A national Hmong organization founded in 1993, working on policy, civic engagement and leadership, affiliated with Hmong American Partnership. Held its 20th national conference in Minneapolis in 2025.

entries.name: SEARAC
entries.purpose: The Southeast Asia Resource Action Center, founded in 1979. National policy advocacy for Cambodian, Laotian and Vietnamese Americans. Its Hmong Census Campaign asks the Census Bureau to classify Hmong as Southeast Asian, not East Asian.

entries.name: Hmong Nurses Association
entries.location: National, based in Elk Grove, California; conferences in St. Paul and Sacramento
entries.purpose: Supports Hmong nurses through mentorship, scholarships and advocacy. Its first national conference was at the University of St. Thomas in 2022, and its third was in St. Paul in August 2026.
entries.linkLabel: IRS filings on ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer

entries.name: Hmong Studies Consortium
entries.location: University of Wisconsin–Madison and University of Minnesota–Twin Cities
entries.purpose: Started in 2009 to promote Hmong scholarship and link researchers. Its seventh international conference was set for October 2026 in Madison.

entries.name: Hmong American Women's Association
entries.type: Domestic violence services and women's leadership
entries.purpose: Founded in 1993 by 13 women in Milwaukee's Hmong refugee community. Provides services for Southeast Asian survivors of domestic violence and sexual assault, along with civic engagement and LGBTQ advocacy.

entries.name: Hmong Innovating Politics
entries.purpose: A grassroots group working to strengthen the political power of Hmong and other disenfranchised communities. Its site lists voter engagement, youth leadership, parent engagement and coalition building. The newest dated activity we saw is a May 2025 blog post, so confirm current programs before referring anyone.

entries.name: Hmong Times
entries.purpose: English and Hmong community news, events and health information.

entries.name: Hmong Radio 1590
entries.location: St. Paul studios; WIXK 1590 AM licensed to New Richmond, Wisconsin, with K294AM 106.7 FM
entries.purpose: Hmong-language music, news and talk for the Twin Cities. Licensed through December 2028. We did not find a station website; the link goes to its FCC record.

entries.name: Hmong Radio AM 690
entries.location: KFXN, licensed to Minneapolis; serves St. Paul
entries.purpose: Hmong news, talk and entertainment, according to a 2020 Radio World report on damage to its studio during protests. Licensed through April 2029. We did not find a station website; the link goes to its FCC record.

entries.name: 3HMONGTV
entries.purpose: Started in 2005 on local cable access. Local, national and global Hmong news, talk and entertainment. It says it began as the Twin Cities' first Hmong television station and has operated for more than 20 years.

entries.name: Crossings TV
entries.purpose: Its site lists Hmong programming. A 2016 Comcast announcement placed it on channel 175 in the Twin Cities, with two hours of Hmong programming on weekdays and four on weekend days. Check the current channel.

entries.name: KBIF 900 AM
entries.purpose: Hmong news, talk, storytelling and farming advice on weekdays, per a 2019 KPBS report. It streams online.

entries.name: Hmong Daily News
entries.purpose: Founded in 2020 by Macy Yang. Hmong diaspora news in English, with a $100,000 Press Forward grant reported in 2024.

entries.name: SBS Hmong
entries.purpose: News and stories in Hmong from Australia's Special Broadcasting Service, available online as a podcast. Added in 2013.

entries.name: Radio Veritas Asia, Hmong Service
entries.purpose: Catholic faith programming for Hmong listeners. It held an Audience Day in northern Thailand in September 2025.
